definition: Refusing to give up or let go, even when things become difficult.
example: The tenacious reporter called the city office every morning until someone finally answered her question.
nuance: Tenacious stresses a firm hold that will not loosen; persistent stresses effort repeated over time.
prompt: A young scientist's experiment keeps failing in the lab.
options: The tenacious scientist rebuilt the setup a dozen times until the results finally held.
The tenacious scientist abandoned the whole project after a single failed trial.
Her evidence was so tenacious and thin that no reviewer found it convincing.
The tenacious scientist mumbled a hesitant guess and then refused to test it again.
reasons: Trying again and again after each failure shows a refusal to quit.
Quitting at the first setback is the reverse of stubborn determination.
Flimsy, weak evidence calls for the look-alike tenuous, not a word about persistence.
Hesitation and giving up suggest someone tentative, not someone who holds firm.

practice.prompt: A small dog has grabbed one end of a rope toy.
options: The puppy had only a tenacious grip, so the rope slipped from its teeth at once.
The tenacious puppy sniffed the rope cautiously, unsure whether to touch it.
The tenacious puppy clung to the rope even when it was lifted off the ground.
The tenacious puppy dropped the rope the moment anyone tugged on it.
reasons: A weak, slipping grip would be tenuous; this word describes a hold that lasts.
Cautious uncertainty fits tentative, not a determined, unshakable grip.
Holding on while dangling in the air shows a grip that will not loosen.
Letting go at the slightest pull shows no firm hold at all.
